blocks.title: What are Standalone Components?
blocks.content: Standalone components declare their own imports directly in the @Component decorator instead of relying on an NgModule. Angular 22 uses standalone as the default and only mode for new applications, removing the need for NgModule boilerplate entirely.
keyPoints: No NgModule is required to declare or bootstrap a standalone component.
Dependencies (directives, pipes, other components) are listed in the `imports` array.
Bootstrapping uses `bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig)` instead of `platformBrowser().bootstrapModule(...)`.

blocks.explanation: The component lists exactly the pieces it needs in `imports`, making dependencies explicit and enabling better tree-shaking.

blocks.question: Why did Angular move away from NgModules toward standalone components?
blocks.answer: To reduce boilerplate, make dependencies explicit per component, simplify lazy loading, and make the mental model closer to how most modern frontend frameworks compose UI.
blocks.explanation: NgModules added an indirection layer that new developers found confusing, and most of what NgModules provided (declarations, providers, exports) can be expressed more directly at the component and provider level.

blocks.mistake: Forgetting to add a directive or pipe to a standalone component's `imports` array.
blocks.whyItHappens: Developers coming from NgModule-based apps assume everything declared anywhere in the app is automatically available.
blocks.correctApproach: Explicitly import every directive, pipe, or component used in the template into the `imports` array of the component that uses it.

blocks.question: You need a route to lazy-load a standalone component that itself depends on three other standalone components and a service. How do you keep that route's chunk from bloating the initial bundle?
blocks.answer: Use `loadComponent: () => import('./feature.component').then(m => m.FeatureComponent)` in the route definition — the dynamic import puts the component and everything it statically imports (its child components, the service) into a separate chunk that only downloads when the route activates.
blocks.explanation: Because a standalone component's dependencies are just regular ES imports declared in its `imports` array, the bundler can trace and split them automatically — there's no NgModule boundary to configure separately, which is part of why standalone components made route-level code-splitting simpler.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would answer this as an architecture and lifecycle problem, not only as an Angular API question. My first decision would be: Begin with dependency analysis and baseline metrics. Identify leaf features with few inbound dependencies and migrate those first.

For implementation, Convert routes and components incrementally. Keep compatibility with existing NgModules where necessary; standalone and module-based code can coexist during migration. Move shared imports into small, purposeful libraries or direct standalone imports. Do not create one global import file that recreates the same coupling problem.

At enterprise scale, I would also cover After each feature, verify route behavior, providers, forms, dialogs, dynamic components, tests, bundle chunks, and production monitoring. Use schematics for mechanical changes, but review generated imports carefully. Add lint rules for circular dependencies and forbidden cross-feature imports.

Finally, Deliver migration in slices with rollback-ready commits and compare build size, initial load, route load, and runtime behavior against the baseline.

I would explicitly discuss provider and state lifetimes, request cancellation, security, accessibility, testability, deployment and rollback. I would avoid adding framework complexity unless the measured scale or ownership model requires it.

I would finish with how I would prove it: targeted unit/component tests, critical end-to-end journeys, production-like profiling, telemetry by route and application version, and measurable before/after results.

title: Lifecycle Hooks
description: The sequence of hooks Angular calls as a component is created, updated, and destroyed.

blocks.title: Component Lifecycle Order
blocks.content: Angular calls lifecycle hooks in a predictable order: constructor, ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit, ngAfterContentChecked, ngAfterViewInit, ngAfterViewChecked, and ngOnDestroy.
keyPoints: ngOnChanges runs before ngOnInit whenever an `@Input()` changes, and on every subsequent input change.
ngOnInit runs once, after the first ngOnChanges.
ngOnDestroy is the place to unsubscribe, clear timers, and release resources.

blocks.explanation: Resources started in ngOnInit are cleaned up in ngOnDestroy to avoid leaking timers after the component is removed.

blocks.question: If a component has no @Input() bindings at all, will ngOnChanges ever run?
blocks.answer: No.
blocks.explanation: ngOnChanges only fires when there is at least one bound @Input() property. Without any inputs, Angular never calls it, so components with no inputs should rely on ngOnInit instead.

blocks.question: Why should you avoid doing heavy DOM or child-component work in the constructor, and put it in ngOnInit instead?
blocks.answer: The constructor runs before Angular has set any @Input() bindings and before the view/child views exist, so anything that depends on input values or ViewChild/ContentChild queries isn't safe yet — ngOnInit runs after the first ngOnChanges, once inputs are populated.
blocks.explanation: A useful mental model: the constructor is for dependency injection only (`private readonly x = inject(X)`), ngOnInit is for initialization logic that needs inputs, and ngAfterViewInit is for logic that needs the rendered view/queried children.

title: Dependency Injection
description: How Angular's hierarchical injector resolves and provides services.

blocks.title: Hierarchical Injectors
blocks.content: Angular resolves a dependency by walking up a tree of injectors: element injector (component/directive), module/environment injector, and the root injector. The first injector in that chain that has a provider for the token wins.
keyPoints: `providedIn: 'root'` registers a singleton in the root environment injector.
Providing a service in a component's `providers` array creates a new instance scoped to that component subtree.
The `inject()` function can be used outside constructors, e.g. in factory functions or field initializers.

blocks.explanation: `inject()` retrieves the current injector's instance of HttpClient without needing a constructor parameter.

blocks.question: Two sibling components each provide the same service in their own `providers` array. Do they share state?
blocks.answer: No, each component subtree gets its own instance.
blocks.explanation: Providing a service at the component level creates a new element injector for that component and its descendants, so each sibling receives an independent instance rather than sharing the root singleton.

blocks.question: What do `@Optional()`, `@Self()`, and `@SkipSelf()` change about how a dependency is resolved?
blocks.answer: `@Optional()` returns null instead of throwing if no provider is found; `@Self()` only looks at the current element's own injector (no walking up the tree); `@SkipSelf()` starts the search at the parent injector, skipping the current element even if it has a matching provider.
blocks.explanation: These decorators are most often seen together in component libraries — e.g. a form control that optionally connects to a parent form group via `@Optional() @SkipSelf() parent?: ControlContainer`, so the component still works standalone when no parent is present.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I use a service when logic or state has a lifecycle and responsibility that should not belong to a presentation component—for example API access, authentication, transaction calculation, logging, feature configuration, or a reusable workflow. A service is not simply a place to move every function; it should expose a cohesive contract and hide implementation details.

Dependency injection gives Angular a controlled way to construct and supply those collaborators. Instead of a component creating HttpClient, a repository, and a logger with new, the component asks for abstractions. Angular's injector resolves them according to provider configuration and scope. This reduces coupling, makes replacement and testing easier, and lets us control whether an instance is application-wide, route-scoped, or component-scoped.

For shared stateless infrastructure, providedIn: 'root' is usually appropriate and tree-shakable. For a feature workflow that must reset when the user leaves a route, I may provide the store at the route level. For isolated component instances, component providers can be correct—but I would explain that this creates a new instance for each component subtree and can accidentally duplicate caches, WebSockets, or token-refresh state.

I use InjectionToken for interfaces, configuration objects, or multiple implementations because TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime. I also keep constructors light: services should not start uncontrolled network calls simply because they were injected. Side effects should begin through explicit methods and be cleaned up according to the provider lifecycle.

In tests, DI lets me substitute a fake repository or logger without changing production code. At architecture level, it also supports ports-and-adapters: domain-facing services depend on small tokens, while infrastructure implementations handle HTTP, storage, and telemetry.
keyPoints: A service groups reusable behavior or state that does not belong to one view, such as API access, caching, authorization, orchestration, or telemetry.
Dependency injection separates object creation from object use. A consumer asks for a contract or token; an injector decides which implementation and lifetime to provide.
This reduces coupling, enables substitution in tests, supports environment-specific implementations, and centralizes lifecycle management.
Provider location defines scope: root for an application singleton, route for feature lifetime, and component for isolated instances. The scope must match ownership of state.
Avoid turning services into global dumping grounds. Keep APIs small, expose read-only state, and isolate side effects.
Use InjectionToken for configuration or interfaces that do not exist at runtime.

title: Change Detection
description: How Angular decides when to re-render a component's view.

blocks.title: Default vs OnPush
blocks.content: In Default mode, Angular checks every component in the tree whenever any asynchronous event Zone.js is aware of occurs (click, timer, HTTP response). In OnPush mode, a component only re-checks when an @Input() reference changes, an event originates from inside the component, or an observable bound with the async pipe emits.
keyPoints: OnPush relies on immutable data: replace objects/arrays rather than mutating them in place.
Signals integrate naturally with OnPush because reading a signal in a template automatically registers it for fine-grained updates.
Zoneless Angular applications skip Zone.js entirely and rely on signals for change notification.

blocks.explanation: Because `percentage` is a signal input, Angular re-renders the interpolation whenever the signal value changes, without needing to check the rest of the component tree.

blocks.question: Explain Default vs OnPush change detection.
blocks.answer: Default checks the whole component tree on every browser event Zone.js patches; OnPush limits checks to input reference changes, internal events, and observable emissions via the async pipe, which is far cheaper for large trees.
blocks.explanation: Use OnPush for presentational components fed with immutable inputs or signals, and reserve Default for components where mutation patterns are hard to avoid.

blocks.mistake: Mutating an array in place (`list.push(item)`) on an OnPush component and expecting the view to update.
blocks.whyItHappens: OnPush compares input references, not deep contents, so mutating the same reference never triggers a check.
blocks.correctApproach: Replace the reference: `this.list = [...this.list, item];` or use a signal and update it with `.set()` / `.update()`.

blocks.question: A component receives data through a third-party callback (e.g. a Google Maps SDK event) that runs outside Angular's Zone.js patched APIs. The view doesn't update even though the underlying data changed. What's happening and how do you fix it?
blocks.answer: Third-party SDKs that schedule their own callbacks (via native timers, WebSockets, or their own event loop) can execute outside Zone.js's monkey-patched APIs, so Angular never gets notified to run change detection. Fix it by explicitly calling `this.ngZone.run(() => { ... })` around the state update, or by injecting `ChangeDetectorRef` and calling `markForCheck()`/`detectChanges()` after the callback.
blocks.explanation: This is the flip side of `NgZone.runOutsideAngular()` — code intentionally run outside the zone (e.g. a high-frequency animation loop) must explicitly re-enter the zone or trigger detection manually to reflect its results in the UI. In zoneless applications this problem disappears for signal-based state, since signal writes notify Angular directly regardless of which zone they happened in.

blocks.content:
I would answer this as an architecture and lifecycle problem, not only as an Angular API question. My first decision would be: Profile first. Confirm that unnecessary change-detection work is material; do not use zoneless mode to hide expensive template functions or large DOM trees.

For implementation, Audit all update sources: signals, event handlers, async pipe, explicit markForCheck, third-party widgets, timers, and custom callbacks. Code that relied only on Zone.js patching may stop updating the view. Migrate a representative feature, add tests for asynchronous rendering, and remove zone.js only after all update paths are explicit.

At enterprise scale, I would also cover Use signals, immutable inputs, OnPush-compatible patterns, and explicit notifications. Wrap incompatible third-party integrations with a small adapter. Compare CPU time, interaction latency, memory, and error reporting before and after. Verify SSR and hydration behavior separately.

Finally, Roll out by application slice with monitoring and a documented fallback.

I would start with evidence, because 'Angular is slow' is not a diagnosis. I would reproduce the slow user journey in a production-like build, record Angular DevTools and Chrome Performance traces, and identify whether the cost comes from network, JavaScript execution, change detection, layout/paint, memory pressure, or oversized assets.

For Angular-specific runtime work, I would inspect which component subtrees are checked frequently and why. I would keep state changes explicit with signals or observable view models, use OnPush where it improves boundaries, avoid template methods that perform work on every check, provide stable identities for repeated rows, and move expensive derived calculations into computed signals or memoized selectors. In an Angular 22 application I would also evaluate zoneless change detection, but only after confirming that third-party libraries and manually scheduled async work notify Angular correctly.

For loading performance, I would split by route, defer heavy below-the-fold components, remove duplicate dependencies, and check parsed/executed JavaScript rather than only compressed bundle size. For very large calculations that are independent of the DOM, I would consider a Web Worker; for large datasets, I would reduce the data before it reaches the browser.

I would make one change at a time and compare the same trace and real-user metric. The final answer should include before/after numbers—for example, reducing a 1.8-second interaction to 180 ms or lowering a route chunk from 1.2 MB to 420 KB—because optimization without measurement can easily move cost somewhere else.
keyPoints: Use Angular DevTools and browser performance traces to identify which components re-render and which computations create long tasks.
Split the page into stable widget boundaries. Use immutable inputs, OnPush or signals, trackBy for repeated views, and computed selectors that return stable references.
Move expensive calculations out of templates. Memoize pure derivations, pre-aggregate data, and schedule non-urgent work when appropriate.
Lazy render off-screen widgets using route splitting, @defer, intersection observers, or virtualization. Destroy inactive charts rather than keeping all canvases alive.
Avoid broad shared-state emissions. Select only the data required by each widget and suppress equivalent emissions.
Set a performance budget and add a repeatable dashboard interaction benchmark to CI.

title: Signals
description: Angular's fine-grained reactive primitive for local and shared state.

blocks.title: Signals vs RxJS
blocks.content: A signal is a synchronous, glitch-free reactive value container: `signal()` holds state, `computed()` derives state, and `effect()` reacts to state changes for side effects. RxJS observables model asynchronous streams and complex event composition (debouncing, retries, combining multiple sources).
keyPoints: Reading a signal inside a template or a `computed()` automatically tracks it as a dependency.
`computed()` values are memoized and only recompute when a dependency changes.
Use `toSignal()` / `toObservable()` from @angular/core/rxjs-interop to bridge the two worlds.

blocks.explanation: `completedCount` recomputes automatically whenever `_progress` changes, without manual subscription management.

blocks.question: Signals vs RxJS: when would you choose one over the other for the Progress Store?
blocks.answer: Signals for synchronous local UI state like progress and bookmarks; RxJS for asynchronous streams like debounced search input or combining multiple HTTP calls.
blocks.explanation: Signals shine for state that is read synchronously in templates; RxJS shines for orchestrating asynchronous, time-based, or multi-source event flows.

blocks.question: You call a signal-writing function inside `effect()`, and the effect also reads that same signal (directly or through a service method). What can go wrong?
blocks.answer: If the write happens as a tracked read-then-write within the same effect execution, the effect becomes dependent on the signal it just wrote to, which re-triggers the effect — potentially in an infinite loop if the written value is never identical to the previous one (e.g. it includes a fresh timestamp).
blocks.explanation: The fix is `untracked()`: wrap the read (or the whole write-path call) so it doesn't register as a dependency of the effect — `untracked(() => this.store.touch(id))`. This is a real, easy-to-hit bug: any service method that reads a signal internally before writing to it becomes unsafe to call from inside an effect unless that internal read is untracked.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would answer this as an architecture and lifecycle problem, not only as an Angular API question. My first decision would be: No. Signals model synchronous reactive state and derived values very well; RxJS models asynchronous event streams, cancellation, retries, time, and complex stream composition.

For implementation, Use signals for component state, computed view models, and fine-grained template updates. Use observables for HTTP pipelines, WebSockets, user-event streams, and orchestration over time. Convert at clear boundaries using toSignal or toObservable rather than repeatedly converting inside components.

At enterprise scale, I would also cover Do not create effects for every derived value; use computed for pure derivation. Keep effects for real side effects such as persistence, analytics, or imperative integration. Define ownership and lifecycle. Avoid hidden subscriptions and avoid writing to several signals from one unstructured effect.

Finally, Measure readability and behavior under cancellation, errors, and rapid updates instead of choosing based on fashion.

I would explicitly discuss provider and state lifetimes, request cancellation, security, accessibility, testability, deployment and rollback. I would avoid adding framework complexity unless the measured scale or ownership model requires it.

I would finish with how I would prove it: targeted unit/component tests, critical end-to-end journeys, production-like profiling, telemetry by route and application version, and measurable before/after results.

title: RxJS switchMap vs mergeMap
description: Choosing the right flattening operator for HTTP calls triggered by user input.

blocks.title: Flattening Operators
blocks.content: switchMap cancels the previous inner observable when a new source value arrives, making it ideal for search-as-you-type. mergeMap runs all inner observables concurrently without cancellation, useful when every request must complete (e.g. batch uploads). concatMap queues inner observables to run strictly in order. exhaustMap ignores new source values while an inner observable is still running.
keyPoints: switchMap: cancel-and-replace (typeahead search).
mergeMap: run concurrently (independent parallel requests).
concatMap: strictly ordered, one at a time (sequential writes).
exhaustMap: ignore new triggers until current completes (prevent duplicate submits).

blocks.explanation: switchMap cancels any in-flight search request as soon as the user types again, so only the latest search's results are ever applied.

blocks.question: Why is switchMap generally preferred over mergeMap for a live search box?
blocks.answer: Because switchMap automatically cancels the previous request, preventing an older, slower response from overwriting the results of a newer search.
blocks.explanation: With mergeMap, if an earlier request resolves after a later one, the UI could flicker back to stale results — a race condition switchMap avoids by cancelling the previous inner subscription.

blocks.question: A "Submit" button triggers an HTTP save on click. Users sometimes double-click it and create two records. Which flattening operator fixes this, and why not switchMap?
blocks.answer: exhaustMap — it ignores new clicks entirely while the in-flight save request hasn't completed, so a rapid second click is simply dropped rather than starting a second request.
blocks.explanation: switchMap would be wrong here: it cancels the *first* request's HTTP call when the second click fires, which for a POST doesn't actually stop the server from processing it — you could still end up with a duplicate record, just with the UI now tracking the wrong response. exhaustMap is the standard idiom for 'prevent duplicate submit' style interactions.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would answer this as an architecture and lifecycle problem, not only as an Angular API question. My first decision would be: Model the filter as a stream and use switchMap so a new filter cancels the previous request subscription.

For implementation, Debounce only where the interaction permits it, apply distinctUntilChanged using a stable query comparison, and keep loading/error state tied to the active request. On the server, still support request cancellation where possible and make responses safe if cancellation arrives late.

At enterprise scale, I would also cover For actions that must not overlap, choose concatMap; for ignoring repeated clicks during one operation, choose exhaustMap; for parallel independent work, choose mergeMap with a concurrency limit. Never solve the problem only by comparing timestamps in the component unless the transport cannot be cancelled.

Finally, Test with delayed responses returned out of order.

I would finish with how I would prove it: targeted unit/component tests, critical end-to-end journeys, production-like profiling, telemetry by route and application version, and measurable before/after results.

title: HTTP Interceptors
description: Intercepting and transforming outgoing requests and incoming responses.

blocks.title: Functional Interceptors
blocks.content: Modern Angular uses functional interceptors registered via `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))`. Each interceptor is a function `(req, next) => Observable<HttpEvent>` that can modify the request, short-circuit it, or transform the response.
keyPoints: Interceptors run in the order they are provided, wrapping each other like middleware.
Common uses: attaching auth headers, logging, global error handling, retry logic.
`next(req)` forwards the (possibly cloned/modified) request to the next interceptor or the backend.

blocks.explanation: This interceptor measures request duration without modifying the request or response payload.

blocks.question: Requests are HTTP objects and immutable. What happens if you try `req.headers.set(...)` directly on the incoming `req`?
blocks.answer: It has no effect on the outgoing request.
blocks.explanation: HttpRequest instances are immutable; `headers.set()` returns a new HttpHeaders object rather than mutating in place. You must clone the request: `req.clone({ headers: req.headers.set('X-Auth', token) })`.

blocks.question: An auth interceptor attaches an access token to every request. The token expires mid-session and the API starts returning 401s. How do you refresh the token and retry the original request transparently, without duplicating the refresh call for every simultaneous 401?
blocks.answer: Catch the 401 in the interceptor with `catchError`, and if a refresh isn't already in flight, call the refresh-token endpoint and share that single Observable (e.g. via `shareReplay(1)`) among all concurrently failing requests; once the refreshed token arrives, clone and retry each original request with the new token using `switchMap`.
blocks.explanation: The key detail interviewers look for is deduplication: without a shared in-flight refresh Observable, five simultaneous 401s would trigger five separate refresh-token calls, and some auth servers invalidate the previous refresh token as soon as a new one is issued, causing a race that logs the user out.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would answer this as an architecture and lifecycle problem, not only as an Angular API question. My first decision would be: Serialize refresh so only one refresh request is active. Queue or replay eligible failed requests after refresh succeeds.

For implementation, Never refresh recursively for the refresh endpoint itself. Distinguish expired credentials from forbidden access, account lock, and backend outages. Prefer secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies when architecture permits; if tokens are held in browser memory, minimize lifetime and avoid persistent storage for sensitive tokens.

At enterprise scale, I would also cover On refresh failure, clear authentication state once, cancel queued work, redirect safely, and preserve only non-sensitive return navigation. Protect state-changing requests against CSRF according to the chosen credential mechanism.

Finally, Test simultaneous failures, slow refresh, logout during refresh, multiple tabs, and clock skew.

I would explicitly discuss provider and state lifetimes, request cancellation, security, accessibility, testability, deployment and rollback. I would avoid adding framework complexity unless the measured scale or ownership model requires it.

I would finish with how I would prove it: targeted unit/component tests, critical end-to-end journeys, production-like profiling, telemetry by route and application version, and measurable before/after results.

title: Optimizing Change Detection for Large Dashboards
description: Senior-level scenario: keeping a real-time dashboard responsive with hundreds of widgets.

blocks.title: Layered Performance Strategy
blocks.content: For a dashboard with hundreds of live-updating widgets, combine several techniques: OnPush on every widget component, immutable data updates (or signals), `track` expressions on @for loops to avoid full DOM re-creation, and splitting the update stream so unrelated widgets don't re-render on every tick.
keyPoints: Use `track widget.id` in @for so Angular reuses DOM nodes instead of recreating them.
Batch incoming real-time updates (e.g. with `bufferTime`) instead of triggering change detection on every single message.
Consider virtual scrolling (CDK Virtual Scroll) when hundreds of widgets are rendered at once but only a handful are visible.

blocks.question: You have a large real-time dashboard where a WebSocket pushes 50 updates/second across 300 widgets. The UI is janky. How would you optimize Angular's change detection here?
blocks.answer: Make every widget OnPush with signal or immutable inputs, buffer/throttle the WebSocket stream so widgets update at a UI-friendly rate (e.g. 10fps) instead of on every message, use `track` for list rendering, and only route each update to the specific widget it affects instead of re-evaluating the whole tree.
blocks.explanation: The goal is to shrink both how often change detection runs and how much of the tree it has to touch each time it does.

blocks.mistake: Subscribing to a shared real-time observable inside every widget component individually.
blocks.whyItHappens: It seems simpler per-component, but it multiplies subscription and change-detection overhead by the number of widgets.
blocks.correctApproach: Subscribe once at a higher level, slice the data per widget with `computed()`/`selectors`, and pass only the relevant slice down as an input.

blocks.question: What does `NgZone.runOutsideAngular()` do, and when would you use it on this dashboard?
blocks.answer: It runs a callback outside Zone.js's patched context, so anything scheduled inside it (timers, event listeners, WebSocket handlers) no longer automatically triggers Angular change detection — you opt back in manually (via `ngZone.run()` or a signal write) only when you actually have something worth rendering.
blocks.explanation: On a dashboard receiving 50 WebSocket messages/second, you'd process and buffer incoming data inside `runOutsideAngular()`, and only re-enter the zone (or update a signal) at the throttled UI update rate — turning 50 potential change-detection passes per second into far fewer.
